entities.summary:
Solidarity, or "Solidarność" in Polish, emerged in 1980 as a pivotal trade union federation in Poland, playing a crucial role in the fight against communist rule. Founded in the Gdańsk Shipyard under the leadership of Lech Wałęsa, it represented not only workers' rights but also a broader anti-authoritarian social movement, which resonated across Eastern Europe. By mobilizing millions, Solidarity became a symbol of resistance against oppressive regimes, galvanizing support from various sectors of society and capturing international attention during a tense period of the Cold War.

The union's early successes included the Gdańsk Agreement of August 1980, which granted workers the right to organize and led to the establishment of independent trade unions in Poland. This breakthrough was significant, as it directly challenged the hegemony of the communist government and inspired similar movements in neighboring countries, ultimately contributing to the fall of the Iron Curtain by the late 1980s. By the time martial law was declared in December 1981, Solidarity had grown to include approximately 10 million members, signifying its profound impact on Polish society and politics.

The legacy of Solidarity is immense; it not only facilitated the transition to democracy in Poland but also served as a catalyst for other anti-communist movements across Eastern Europe, including the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia and the protests in Hungary. The Round Table Talks in 1989 between the government and Solidarity representatives resulted in partially free elections, marking the beginning of the end for communist rule in the region. Solidarity's influence persists today, as it continues to inspire contemporary labor movements and political activism worldwide, symbolizing the enduring quest for freedom and justice.
